title: Ezekiel 39:21–29
context: The LORD says he will set his glory among the nations, who will see his judgment and understand that Israel went into exile because of its own iniquity, not because its God was weak. Now he will restore Jacob, have mercy on the whole house of Israel, and gather them so they live securely with no one to make them afraid. He will no longer hide his face from them, “for I have poured out my Spirit on the house of Israel.” Ezekiel 36:27, 37:14, and Joel 2:28 speak of God’s Spirit in related ways, each in its own setting. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about God’s faithfulness through judgment and restoration.

verses.text: “I will set my glory among the nations. Then all the nations will see my judgment that I have executed, and my hand that I have laid on them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will set his glory among the nations, and all will see his judgment and his hand laid on them. The purpose turns to revelation.

Arminian readers see God making himself known to all peoples.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse moves from the defeat of Gog to its meaning for the nations.

Reformed readers see God displaying his glory through judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s purpose to make his glory known among the nations through his acts in history.

verses.text: So the house of Israel will know that I am the LORD their God, from that day and forward.
verses.arminianNotes:
The house of Israel will know that the LORD is their God from that day forward. Israel’s knowledge of God is lasting.

Arminian readers see a renewed and continuing relationship with God following his deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase “from that day and forward” suggests a decisive turning point.

Reformed readers see God securing his people’s knowledge of him. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s faithfulness bringing his people to know him, whatever their views about the timing of the events described.

verses.text: The nations will know that the house of Israel went into captivity for their iniquity, because they trespassed against me, and I hid my face from them; so I gave them into the hand of their adversaries, and they all fell by the sword.
verses.arminianNotes:
The nations will know that Israel went into captivity for its iniquity, because it trespassed and God hid his face and gave it to its enemies. The exile is explained.

Arminian readers see exile as the consequence of Israel’s chosen unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse corrects any idea that Israel’s God was too weak to protect them.

Reformed readers see God’s justice in the exile. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: I did to them according to their uncleanness and according to their transgressions. I hid my face from them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says he dealt with them according to their uncleanness and transgressions and hid his face from them. Judgment fit the sin.

Arminian readers see consequences matching the people’s conduct.
verses.reformedNotes:
The language of hiding the face recalls covenant warnings such as Deuteronomy 31:17.

Reformed readers see God’s righteous dealing with sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the justice of the exile and the seriousness of covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: “Therefore the Lord GOD says: ‘Now I will reverse the captivity of Jacob and have mercy on the whole house of Israel. I will be jealous for my holy name.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD will now reverse Jacob’s captivity and have mercy on the whole house of Israel, being jealous for his holy name. Mercy follows judgment.

Arminian readers see God’s gracious restoration of his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
God’s jealousy for his name is the ground of the restoration here, as in 36:22.

Reformed readers see mercy grounded in God’s own purposes. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s mercy to his people after judgment.

verses.text: They will forget their shame and all their trespasses by which they have trespassed against me, when they dwell securely in their land. No one will make them afraid
verses.arminianNotes:
They will forget their shame and trespasses when they live securely in their land, with no one to make them afraid. Restoration brings peace.

Arminian readers see a renewed people living in safety.
verses.reformedNotes:
Readers differ on whether forgetting shame means release from disgrace or a lifting of its weight. The verse in any case links security with God’s restoration.

Reformed readers see God’s gracious renewal. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the sense hedged.

verses.text: when I have brought them back from the peoples, gathered them out of their enemies’ lands, and am shown holy among them in the sight of many nations.
verses.arminianNotes:
This will happen when God brings them back from the peoples and gathers them from their enemies’ lands, and is shown holy among them before many nations. The return displays God’s holiness.

Arminian readers see restoration as a public witness to the nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse echoes 36:23–24, where God also gathers his people and shows himself holy.

Reformed readers see God’s holiness displayed through his acts. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: They will know that I am the LORD their God, in that I caused them to go into captivity among the nations, and have gathered them to their own land. Then I will leave none of them captive any more.
verses.arminianNotes:
They will know the LORD is their God, who sent them into captivity and gathered them to their land, leaving none captive. Both exile and return reveal him.

Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness in judgment and mercy alike.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse holds together God’s action in both exile and return.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign hand in both. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s faithfulness through judgment and restoration, which together lead his people to know him.

verses.text: I won’t hide my face from them any more, for I have poured out my Spirit on the house of Israel,’ says the Lord GOD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will no longer hide his face, “for I have poured out my Spirit on the house of Israel.” Arminian readers see the Spirit’s renewing grace, received and continued by faith.

The boxes at Deuteronomy 5:29 and 10:16 treat this; see also Deuteronomy 30:6. Compare Ezekiel 36:27.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s Spirit securing his people’s renewal.

Joel 2:28 speaks of God pouring out his Spirit in its own setting, and Ezekiel 37:14 promises his Spirit to Israel. Both traditions read the promise as God’s gracious gift.
